problems.question: Manganese has seven outer electrons beyond its argon core. How are they arranged at the lowest energy?

options.label: 4s² 3d⁵, with one electron in each 3d orbital

problems.explanation: In a neutral atom, 4s fills first and 3d fills singly before pairing. Five 3d electrons put one unpaired electron in each of the five 3d orbitals.

problems.question: Neutral nickel has outer electrons 4s² 3d⁸. What is the electron arrangement of the Ni²⁺ ion?
problems.explanation: Once a metal becomes a positive ion, 3d drops below 4s, so the two 4s electrons leave first and Ni²⁺ keeps all eight 3d electrons.

problems.question: Magnesium's first three ionization energies are 738, 1451, and 7733 kJ/mol. Which ion does magnesium form?
problems.explanation: The ionization energy jumps more than fivefold at the third electron because it comes from a full inner shell, so magnesium loses two electrons to form Mg²⁺.

problems.question: Neutral scandium is 4s² 3d¹, and its only common ion is Sc³⁺. Is scandium a transition metal by the definition used here?

options.label: No: Sc³⁺ has no 3d electrons left
Yes: its neutral atom has a 3d electron
No: it is not in the fourth row

problems.explanation: Sc³⁺ has lost all three outer electrons, leaving its 3d subshell empty. Under our definition, a transition metal must form at least one ion with a partly filled 3d subshell (though some textbooks also count elements whose neutral atoms have partly filled d subshells).

problems.question: What is the overall charge of a complex ion made of one Co³⁺ ion, four NH₃ molecules, and two Cl− ions?
problems.explanation: Ammonia is neutral (0), so the overall charge is +3 from Co³⁺ plus two −1 chloride ions: +3 − 2 = +1, giving [Co(NH₃)₄Cl₂]⁺.

problems.question: Oxalate (C₂O₄²−) bonds to a metal ion through two oxygen atoms. How many oxalate ions fill six spots around Fe³⁺, and what is the overall charge?
problems.explanation: Each oxalate takes two spots, so three fill all six. Three −2 ions combined with Fe³⁺ give +3 − 6 = −3, forming [Fe(C₂O₄)₃]³−.

problems.question: In an octahedral complex with five NH₃ and one Cl−, how many different arrangements exist?
problems.explanation: All six positions on an octahedron are identical. Rotating the complex turns any single Cl− placement into any other, so there is only one arrangement.

problems.question: Why does a tetrahedral complex with two NH₃ and two Cl− have no cis or trans isomers?

options.label: Every pair of positions in a tetrahedron is the same angle apart
A tetrahedron only holds two ligands
Chloride cannot bond to a tetrahedral ion
All four ligands lie in one flat plane

problems.explanation: Every position in a tetrahedron is 109.5° from every other position, so there is no difference between side by side and opposite. Every placement is the same molecule rotated.

problems.question: A nickel(II) complex solution absorbs red light. What colour does the solution look?
problems.explanation: You see the light that passes through. Green sits opposite red on the colour wheel, so a solution that absorbs red looks green.

problems.question: Ligand X creates a wider d-orbital gap than ligand Y. Which complex absorbs shorter-wavelength light?
problems.explanation: A wider gap requires higher-energy photons, and higher-energy photons have shorter wavelengths.

worked.title: The gap from a wavelength
worked.setup: A chromium(III) complex absorbs 575 nm light. Find its d-orbital gap in kJ/mol. Use h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, and Nₐ = 6.02 × 10²³ /mol.

steps.say: What is the energy of one 575 nm photon, in units of 10⁻¹⁹ J?
steps.hint: Use E = hc ÷ λ with λ in metres: 575 nm = 575 × 10⁻⁹ m.

steps.say: What is the energy of one mole of these photons, in J/mol?
steps.hint: Multiply one photon's energy by Avogadro's number.

steps.say: Titanium's gap is 239 kJ/mol. How does this chromium complex's gap compare?
steps.explain: 208 kJ/mol is smaller than 239 kJ/mol, so the gap is narrower and it absorbs longer-wavelength light.

worked.finish: A complex's energy gap matches the absorbed photon's energy: E = hc ÷ λ for one photon, multiplied by Avogadro's number for one mole.

problems.question: When the crystal field gap is wider than the pairing cost, how do six d electrons arrange themselves?

options.label: All six pair up in the lower three orbitals, leaving none unpaired (low spin).
Five spread singly across all five orbitals and the sixth pairs below (four unpaired).
Four fill the upper two orbitals first, leaving two below.
All six leave the ion because the gap is too wide.

problems.explanation: Electrons take the lowest-energy arrangement. When crossing the gap costs more than pairing, all six pair up in the lower three orbitals.

problems.question: A manganese(II) water complex has five unpaired d electrons, while a nickel(II) water complex has two. How do their magnetic pulls compare?

options.label: The manganese(II) complex is pulled more strongly toward a magnet.
The nickel(II) complex is pulled more strongly toward a magnet.
Both are pulled equally because both are +2 ions.
Neither is pulled because water cancels unpaired electrons.

problems.explanation: Magnetic pull grows stronger with more unpaired electrons, so five unpaired electrons produce a stronger pull than two.

problems.question: What is the overall charge of a complex ion formed by Co³⁺, five neutral NH₃ molecules, and one Cl− ion?
problems.explanation: Co³⁺ (+3) plus five neutral NH₃ (0) and one Cl− (−1) gives an overall charge of +2.

problems.question: Both [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ and [Fe(CN)₆]³− contain Fe³⁺ (five d electrons). Why is [Fe(H₂O)₆]³⁺ pulled harder by a magnet?

options.label: Water makes a narrower gap, leaving all five d electrons unpaired, whereas cyanide's wide gap pairs four of them.
Water adds an extra electron to iron(III), raising the count to six.
Cyanide removes all d electrons from iron(III).

problems.explanation: High-spin Fe³⁺ with water has five unpaired electrons, while low-spin Fe³⁺ with cyanide has only one.
